title: Ring homomorphisms and evaluation
section: Part B: Abstract Algebra ▷ Ring Homomorphisms
terms: ring homomorphism; ring endomorphism; evaluation homomorphism; substitution homo- morphism; kernel of a ring homomorphism; unital homomorphism.

exposition.text:
A ring homomorphism preserves addition and multiplication, hence zero and additive inverses.
The book does not require preservation of unity; a unital homomorphism additionally sends 1
to 1. Under the nonunital convention, both the zero map and identity map are endomorphisms
of Z. Kernels and images are additive subgroups and subrings.
For a commutative ring R, evaluation R[x] → R, f 7→ f(a), is a homomorphism. For a non-
commutative coefficient ring this requires a to commute with coefficients; it is not automatic. A
homomorphism Z → R is determined by the idempotent image of 1. Preserving one operation
alone, as with the additive map n 7→ 2n, does not make a ring homomorphism.
For m, n > 1, a unital map Z → Z exists exactly when n | m; it is then reduction of residue
m n
classes. The determinant on a full matrix ring is multiplicative but generally not additive. Com-
plex conjugation preserves both operations and is a ring automorphism. Evaluation at a matrix
fixes all coefficients, so its substituted matrix must commute with each coefficient.

question.text:
Let E : Q[x] → Q evaluate polynomials at x = 3. Which polynomial generates its kernel as an
ideal?
2
(A) x (B) x − 3 (C) x − 9 (D) x + 3 (E) 3x

solution.text:
The factor theorem says f(3) = 0 exactly when x − 3 divides f(x). Thus the kernel is the
2
ideal of all multiples of x − 3. The larger-degree polynomial x − 9 does not generate every
such multiple.

question.text:
Which condition on positive integers m, n > 1 is necessary and sufficient for a unital ring homo-
morphism Z → Z to exist?
m n
(A) gcd(m, n) = 1
(B) m | n
(C) n | m
(D) m = n
(E) m and n are both prime

solution.text:
A unital map must send the class of k to the class of k, since it preserves addition and 1.
The relation m · 1 = 0 in the domain therefore requires m = 0 modulo n. Conversely, when
n | m, reduction modulo n is well defined and preserves both operations and unity.

question.text:
Which of the following maps preserve both addition and multiplication?
I. Z → Z, n 7→ 2n.
II. M (R) → R, A 7→ det A.
2
III. C → C, z 7→ z.
(A) I only (B) II only (C) III only (D) I and III only (E) II and III only

solution.text:
For I, the images of 1 · 1 and the product of the images are 2 and 4. For II, det(I + I) = 4
but det I + det I = 2. Complex conjugation preserves sums and products, so III is a ring au-
tomorphism. Preserving just the additive or multiplicative structure is insufficient.
